idiom_name: companion object apply factory (object Shape { def apply(...) })
implementation_notes: Scala's own documentation states it directly: an apply method in the companion object acts as a Factory Method, and the language's sugar turns Shape(...) into Shape.apply(...), so callers never write new (docs.scala-lang.org, Companion Objects). What replaces the classic Creator subclass is that overloaded apply set, which may declare a broader result type and return any subtype (the standard library's Array companion is a catalogue of factory methods) and may return Option/Either when construction can fail - Email.fromString returning Option[Email] is the documented example. The classic protected create() in an abstract class is still expressible and is used where a framework subclasses the creator.
pitfalls: Companion object and class must be defined in the same file; splitting them is a compile error about missing companions, not a runtime surprise.
apply overloads are resolved statically on argument types, so a String-keyed factory loses the checking that a sealed/enum parameter would give - a typo becomes a run-time IllegalArgumentException.
Case classes already generate an apply in their companion; adding a same-signature overload creates ambiguity or shadows the synthetic one.
A factory that throws for unknown input forces callers into exception handling; Option/Either-returning factories (or a sealed input type) keep failures in the type system.
